Multiway compositional (CoDa) model of life-table deaths for subpopulations

Source: R/model-coda-multiway.R
coda_multiway.Rd

coda_multiway() is the three-way compositional model of Bergeron-Boucher, Simonacci, Oeppen and Gallo (2018): a Tucker3 decomposition of the centred log-ratios of the life-table deaths of several populations, with time indexes shared by all of them. The strata are the populations (for example the regions of a country). Status: published, with the choices listed below where the paper leaves the method open. Section and equation numbers refer to that paper. The model is experimental: compare it with coda() (coherent = TRUE) and li_lee() in a backtest before using it.

Usage

coda_multiway(
  ranks = c(1, 1, 1),
  order = c(0, 1, 0),
  drift = TRUE,
  jump_off = c("fitted", "observed"),
  open = c("auto", "kannisto", "regression")
)

Arguments

ranks

Numbers of components c(age, time, population), by default c(1, 1, 1). They are reduced where the data allow fewer components (at most the number of parts of the composition minus 1, of years minus 1 and of populations, and no rank above the product of the other two), with a warning (class mt_warning_argument) that names the requested and the ranks used; the label of the fit and mt_parameters() (rank) give the ranks used.

order

ARIMA order c(p, d, q) of each time index; c(0, 1, 0) by default (random walk, Bergeron-Boucher et al. 2018, Section 5).

drift

Include a drift when d = 1; ignored otherwise (d = 0 includes a mean, d = 2 no constant).

jump_off

"fitted" (forecasts start from the fitted deaths) or "observed" (from the observed deaths of the last year).

open

Treatment of the old ages: "auto" (the Kannisto extension where the age groups allow it, otherwise the regression of the open interval), "kannisto" or "regression", as in coda().

Value

A model specification.

Details

Model (Section 2.2, eq. 5). For population i:

  1. the death rates of each year give life-table deaths d[x, t, i] with radix 1 at the first age (life_table() conventions), as in coda();

  2. a[x, i] is the geometric mean of d[x, t, i] over the years, closed to 1;

  3. the deaths are centred by perturbation (d[x, t, i] / a[x, i], closed) and transformed by the centred log-ratio (clr), eq. (3);

  4. the array of centred log-ratios [age, year, population] follows the Tucker3 model clr(d[x, t, i] / a[x, i]) = sum_pqr g[p, q, r] b[x, p] k[t, q] gamma[i, r], with age patterns b, time indexes k and population markers gamma (the paper's beta, kappa and gamma), each of unit length, and the core array g; ranks = c(P, Q, R) gives the numbers of components of age, time and population. The default c(1, 1, 1) is the model of the paper's forecasts (Sections 4 and 5);

  5. the time index follows a random walk with drift (order = c(0, 1, 0), drift = TRUE), the ARIMA model that the paper selected by AIC for the index of Canadian women (Section 5);

  6. forecasts are transformed back (inverse clr, perturbation by a[x, i], closure) to life-table deaths and then to death rates.

With one component per mode, population i changes by g gamma[i] b[x] k[t]: all populations follow one index and one age pattern, at a pace set by their markers. The forecasts are coherent in this sense; populations with different markers keep changing at different paces (Section 5.1). With one population, the fit and the point forecasts are those of coda() with the same index model and jump-off; the draws of coda() also carry the uncertainty of the estimates.

Estimation (Sections 2.2 and 4). Least squares by alternating least squares: higher-order orthogonal iteration (De Lathauwer, De Moor and Vandewalle 2000), started from the higher-order singular value decomposition. The paper uses the Tucker3 model for compositional data of Gallo (2015), an alternating least-squares algorithm for the same criterion. The clr of a composition sums to zero and the centring removes the mean over the years, so b and k sum to zero. Signs: each time index increases over the fitting period, each set of population markers has a positive sum, and the largest core element of each age pattern is positive; with one component, life-table deaths then move from ages with negative b to ages with positive b as k rises. fit$fits$fit_pct is the share of the sum of squares of the centred array that the model explains (the explained variance of Section 4.1), fit$fits$core_pct the share of each core element.

Draws (Section 5). The paper draws its prediction intervals from simulations of the time index with resampled errors. Here each time index is simulated from its ARIMA model with innovations resampled from its residuals; a, b, gamma, g and the drift are fixed, and the draws of the index are shared by all populations. Draws are expected rates; predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates and the exposures, and no other observation noise.

Choices where the paper is silent.

  • Jump-off: the paper states no adjustment, so forecasts start from the fitted deaths (jump_off = "fitted"). jump_off = "observed" starts each population from its observed deaths of the last year, perturbed by the change of the model, as in coda() (Bergeron-Boucher, Canudas-Romo, Oeppen and Vaupel 2017, Appendix G).

  • Several time indexes (ranks[2] > 1): the paper forecasts with one index. Each index then has its own ARIMA model, independent of the others, as for several components of a CoDa model in Shang and Haberman (2020).

  • Other ARIMA orders (order, drift): the point forecast of an ARIMA(0,1,q) index with drift gets the first-step correction of coda() (Bergeron-Boucher et al. 2017, eq. 20); its draws are shifted by the same amount.

  • Old ages and zero deaths, as in coda(): with single-year age groups from 80 (open = "auto" or "kannisto"), the rates from age 80 come from a Kannisto model fitted per year and population and extended to age 120 (Bergeron-Boucher et al. 2017, Appendix C); with other age groups, the log death rate of the open interval of each population is regressed on the time indexes (package-specific). Zero deaths are replaced multiplicatively (Bergeron-Boucher et al. 2017, Appendix C). The paper uses five-year age groups to 100+ and five-year periods and combines the smallest populations to avoid zero counts; the models of this package need single calendar years.

  • Strata of a hierarchy (see mt_aggregate_strata()) enter the decomposition as populations of their own; reconciled() makes their sums coherent.

The paper chooses the numbers of components by the DifFit criterion (Timmerman and Kiers 2000), gives bootstrap confidence intervals of the parameters (Kiers 2004) and compares models by the AIC of Poisson deviances (Table 2); these are not implemented. It fits women and men separately, as stratified("sex", female = coda_multiway(), male = coda_multiway()) does.

References

Bergeron-Boucher M-P, Simonacci V, Oeppen J, Gallo M (2018). Coherent modeling and forecasting of mortality patterns for subpopulations using multiway analysis of compositions: an application to Canadian provinces and territories. North American Actuarial Journal 22(1): 92-118. doi:10.1080/10920277.2017.1377620

Bergeron-Boucher M-P, Canudas-Romo V, Oeppen J, Vaupel JW (2017). Coherent forecasts of mortality with compositional data analysis. Demographic Research 37(17): 527-566. doi:10.4054/DemRes.2017.37.17

Gallo M (2015). Tucker3 model for compositional data. Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods 44(21): 4441-4453. doi:10.1080/03610926.2013.798664

Shang HL, Haberman S (2020). Forecasting age distribution of death counts: an application to annuity pricing. Annals of Actuarial Science 14(1): 150-169. doi:10.1017/S1748499519000101

De Lathauwer L, De Moor B, Vandewalle J (2000). On the best rank-1 and rank-(R1, R2, ..., RN) approximation of higher-order tensors. SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications 21(4): 1324-1342. doi:10.1137/S0895479898346995

Timmerman ME, Kiers HAL (2000). Three-mode principal components analysis: choosing the numbers of components and sensitivity to local optima. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology 53(1): 1-16. doi:10.1348/000711000159132

Kiers HAL (2004). Bootstrap confidence intervals for three-way methods. Journal of Chemometrics 18(1): 22-36. doi:10.1002/cem.841

See also

coda() for one population and for the coherent model with a common component and deviations, tucker3() for the three-way model of log death rates.

Examples

x <- mt_example_regions(years = 2000:2015, regions = 3)
fit <- mt_fit(coda_multiway(), x)
fit$fits$fit_pct
#> [1] 38.67032
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 5, n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
